verses.text: When Saul had returned from following the Philistines, he was told, “Behold, David is in the wilderness of En Gedi.”
Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and went to seek David and his men on the rocks of the wild goats.
He came to the sheep pens by the way, where there was a cave; and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were staying in the innermost parts of the cave.

David’s men said to him, “Behold, the day of which Yahweh said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.’” Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe secretly.
Afterward, David’s heart struck him, because he had cut off Saul’s skirt.
He said to his men, “Yahweh forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, Yahweh’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is Yahweh’s anointed.”
So David checked his men with these words, and didn’t allow them to rise against Saul. Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way.
David also arose afterward, and went out of the cave, and cried after Saul, saying, “My lord the king!” When Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth, and showed respect.
David said to Saul, “Why do you listen to men’s words, saying, ‘Behold, David seeks to harm you?’

Behold, today your eyes have seen how Yahweh had delivered you today into my hand in the cave. Some urged me to kill you; but I spared you; and I said, I will not stretch out my hand against my lord; for he is Yahweh’s anointed.

Moreover, my father, behold, yes, see the skirt of your robe in my hand; for in that I cut off the skirt of your robe, and didn’t kill you, know and see that there is neither evil nor disobedience in my hand, and I have not sinned against you, though you hunt for my life to take it.
May Yahweh judge between me and you, and may Yahweh avenge me of you; but my hand will not be on you.
As the proverb of the ancients says, ‘Out of the wicked comes wickedness;’ but my hand will not be on you.
Against whom has the king of Israel come out? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog? A flea?
May Yahweh therefore be judge, and give sentence between me and you, and see, and plead my cause, and deliver me out of your hand.”
It came to pass, when David had finished speaking these words to Saul, that Saul said, “Is that your voice, my son David?” Saul lifted up his voice, and wept.
He said to David, “You are more righteous than I; for you have done good to me, whereas I have done evil to you.
You have declared today how you have dealt well with me, because when Yahweh had delivered me up into your hand, you didn’t kill me.
For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away unharmed? Therefore may Yahweh reward you good for that which you have done to me today.
Now, behold, I know that you will surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hand.
Swear now therefore to me by Yahweh, that you will not cut off my offspring  after me, and that you will not destroy my name out of my father’s house.”
David swore to Saul. Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.

footnotes.content: Saul turns from chasing Philistines to chase David—fear and pride still rule his heart. How often we turn from our true enemy to target those who don't threaten us at all. David's wilderness refuge was meant to be safe; instead, Saul's obsession brings pursuit there too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three thousand men to hunt one man and his followers—Saul throws the whole weight of the kingdom at David. Sometimes our fear makes us wasteful, deploying far more than we need, as if sheer force could settle what only trust can heal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A cave near En Gedi, and Saul comes in to relieve himself—the very picture of vulnerability. David and his men hidden in the shadows watch their hunter become helpless. The Lord's hand works quietly in small moments when our guard is down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's men see what looks like God's moment—a divine delivery, they think. But David cuts only the robe's hem, not the man. He obeys what he knows is true over what his eyes seem to show him. This is the quiet strength we need most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His heart smites him—even that small cutting of Saul's garment troubles David's conscience. A tender heart is a guard against creeping toward wrong, even in small steps. What troubles us when no one watches shows us who we truly are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's anointed—David speaks this twice, holding fast to what God declared even when Saul has betrayed that trust. To honor the office even when the man has fallen is to honor the Lord who placed him there. Our loyalty to God's work outlasts our anger at those who hold it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's words checked his men—they wanted vengeance, they saw the chance, but a quieter voice held them back. One faithful person standing firm can turn a whole company from a path they've begun. This is the power of conviction spoken at the right moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After Saul leaves the cave, David runs after him calling out, bowing with his face to the earth. He could have let his enemy walk away free and never know; instead, David chooses to be seen. The truth told in humility is braver than silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David asks why Saul listens to whispered words about him—the complaint of one hunted, but also a deeper question: why do we believe the worst of those we fear? A word spoken in anger finds an eager ear in a troubled heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David shows the robe's hem—evidence that he could have killed Saul but did not. He holds out his restraint like a mirror, hoping Saul will see what mercy looks like. Sometimes we must show our goodness clearly, not hide it, so others can learn the shape of grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In that I cut off the skirt of your robe, and didn't kill you—David dwells on the skirt, the one small proof of his power and his choice. By what we do NOT do, others know us. Our restraint, held when we could act, is the clearest word we speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Let Yahweh judge between me and you—David hands the matter to the Lord. He has shown restraint, told the truth, and now he lets go. There is a freedom in refusing to fight our own battles when we know we are right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The proverb of the ancients: out of the wicked comes wickedness—David speaks a truth known long before his time. He is saying, I will not be like you; I will not let your wickedness make me wicked. To refuse the pattern we see in others is to break a chain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A dead dog, a flea—David speaks with a kind of gentle mockery, pointing out the true size of the thing Saul hunts. When we stand before the Lord, how small our quarrels become. What looms so large in our rage looks so small from a higher place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David turns again to Yahweh to judge and plead his cause. He does not ask for his own hand to do the work, but for the Lord's. This is the prayer of one who trusts that being in the right is enough, if the Lord knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Is that your voice, my son David?—Saul hears, and something in him breaks. Tears come. A moment's grace touches a hardened heart when the truth is spoken plainly and without malice. We never know when our humble word will crack a wall we thought was sealed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You are more righteous than I—Saul admits it. In a moment of clarity, he sees what David has shown him: the difference between vengeance and mercy, between grasping and letting go. Sometimes we need to see it lived before we understand it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You declared today how you have dealt well with me—Saul names the deed. David's action has a voice all its own now. The clearest sermon is sometimes the one we preach without words, by what we do when no one would know if we didn't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away unharmed?—Saul asks the very question his culture would answer no to. Yet David has done it. Saul can feel the weight of it: kindness shown when cruelty was expected is its own kind of argument.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now I know you will surely be king—Saul's resistance breaks fully. He releases his grip, admits the truth he has fought. When the Lord has decided a thing, no amount of our striving will change it; wisdom lies in accepting and blessing what we cannot stop.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Swear to me that you will not cut off my offspring—Saul's last concern is for his sons. In a moment of grace, he thinks beyond himself. Even as he lets David go, he asks for mercy for those he loves. The Lord often plants that seed in us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David swore to Saul, and Saul went home—a moment of peace between two men God held apart. Readers today hear an echo in this: mercy given and received can pause even the deepest conflict. It does not always resolve everything, but it reminds both of us that we are more than our enmity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
